Today, UNCDF is reinvigorated to fulfill its unique role in the UN development system, that of channeling supplementary capital to countries that are furthest behind in their development aspirations. UNCDF is presently one of only 2 UN entities that can provide financial de-risking with the appropriate instruments needed to stimulate underdeveloped markets. What makes UNCDF different and, to date, underleveraged is that, unlike AAA-rated financial institutions that find it difficult to accommodate more than a 1% expected loss UNCDF can. Why? Because we do not borrow. We have no balance sheet to protect. Our role is to absorb risks that others in finance cannot easily do, and to catalyze development finance that otherwise would escape communities in last-mile conditions. The renewed focus of our mission is simple but vital. To reduce financial risks to unlock investments where capital traditionally does not flow to. This means lifting early-stage innovators and small businesses and fueling economic growth and prosperity for underserved communities in high-risk markets. In today's context, where official development assistance is declining, this mission is more critical than ever. According to Convergence, less than 5%— 5%— of global financial assets are invested in developing countries, with only a fraction of that making its way to least developed countries, most of which are in Africa and small island states. So as we prepare for the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development, UNCDF stands ready to help rethink how development finance can reach the last mile, and how to truly crowd in private capital for development. UNCDF exists to do exactly that. Now, our results in the 2022-2024 period give us reason for optimism. UNCDF has positively impacted the lives of nearly 30 million people in underserved areas. We have enabled access to energy for off-grid communities, expanded digital financial services to unbanked individuals and businesses, and supported climate risk management in vulnerable regions, from small islands to rural Africa. In just 3 years, we have supported over 500,000 small-medium-sized enterprises, exceeding our strategic target. These are job creators in frontier markets and critical in areas with young populations. Our catalytic use of grants, loans, and guarantees, and the technical advisory support that we provide, has mobilized more than $780 million in additional investment against an annual core that has been less than $10 million. We're now better positioned to complement the UN Development System and multilateral development banks aligned with the 2024 Q CPR resolution that calls for greater coherence, synergy, and complementarity among development actors. Let me share two examples of what this looks like in practice. In Nigeria, we have partnered with UNICEF to combat child malnutrition by investing two and a half million in local producers of therapeutic foods. It's not the amount that is important here, but. what this has done. This has not only saved lives, but it has stimulated local agriculture, it has created jobs, and it has reduced resilience— reliance, rather, on imports, thereby reducing the burden on foreign exchange reserves that are scarce. In Afghanistan, UNCDF, together with UNDP and the Resident Coordinator's Office, teamed up to deploy a financial guarantee to unlock more than $7 million of capital for hundreds of MSMEs, critical in a country where SMEs employ 90% of the workforce. Now, to fully realize UNCDF's potential, we have to address 3 key issues. First, we need to scale up our capital investments. In 2024, only a quarter of our resources were deployed as loans or guarantees. This needs to change; it needs to be much higher. Now, we've adopted a new investment policy and process, we've strengthened our digital systems, and we're introducing AI and blockchain technology to be able to deploy smaller amounts of capital more frequently and faster. In crisis settings, which we are working on with UNDP's Crisis Bureau, our goal is to deploy capital in 21 days, making us one of the fastest-moving capital providers to MSMEs in fragile contexts. Second, we need to strengthen our fiduciary oversight in line with our growth ambitions. Our core contributions amounted to less than $7 million, still far short of the $25 million target that the Board has endorsed. Core funds now make up just 6% of our total resources. Constraining our ability to be more strategic, to be more responsive. We also had success on our non-core contributions last year of about $112 million, so I seek the support of the Board to really unlock additional core as well as non-core so that we can augment support to LDCs. I know this is a difficult task in today's context, but it's critical. Third, we are relocating closer to where we operate. We are also in dialogue with member states about potentially relocating our headquarters to further strengthen partnerships with DFIs impact investors and donors who have historically invested the most in UNCDF, including the EU, Germany, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK, and Norway. This next chapter will reflect your Member States' demand for a catalytic vehicle to mobilize private sector finance in difficult and challenged markets, first and foremost in LDCs. It will define our role not as a competitor to the MDBs or the DFIs, but as an enabler of a broader development finance architecture where money flows must be to those that most need it. I'm encouraged by the growing recognition of our unique value proposition. UNCDF is now working along partners such as UNDP, UNV, UNICEF, WFP, the International Finance Corporation, Mitsubishi Financial Group, Standard Chartered, and insurance leaders like Aon and Lloyd's. We are also advancing our EU Pillar assessment, on track to become the second UN entity to access the EU gateway for the deployment of guarantees. We have momentum, but to meet the scale of the challenge, UNCDF must be properly capitalized with larger volumes of flexible, unearmarked resources. This is a moment of transformation, not just for UNCDF, but for how the UN system meets the needs of the world's most vulnerable economies. As the Associate Administrator has noted, a dollar invested in UNCDF is recycled, leveraged, and multiplied, reaching where others cannot.
